lessons.title: async/await Basics

quickCheck.prompt: What does `await` do at a suspension point?
quickCheck.explanation: `await` pauses the task and releases the thread to the scheduler — the thread is free for other work while the result is pending. This is not a blocking wait.

options.text: Suspends the current task, freeing the thread for other work
Blocks the current thread until the result is ready
Creates a new thread
Calls DispatchQueue.main.async

lessons.title: Actors & Data Isolation

quickCheck.prompt: How does an actor prevent data races?
quickCheck.explanation: Actors serialize access to their mutable state — the runtime queues concurrent callers and lets only one execute at a time, eliminating unsynchronized shared-state writes.

options.text: By running all code on a single background thread
By serializing access to its mutable state — only one caller executes at a time
By making all properties constants
By using locks internally

lessons.title: Tasks & Structured Concurrency
lessons.body:
Swift provides several ways to launch concurrent work, each with different lifetime and actor-inheritance rules.

### `Task { }` vs `Task.detached`

`Task { }` inherits the current actor context and priority. `Task.detached { }` starts fresh — no actor, no priority inherited. Use detached only when you explicitly want to escape the surrounding context.

### `async let` — parallel child tasks

`async let` starts a child task immediately but defers the `await` until you need the value. Multiple `async let` bindings run in **parallel**.

```swift
async let profile = fetchProfile(id: userID)
async let feed   = fetchFeed(id: userID)

let (p, f) = try await (profile, feed)  // both ran in parallel
```

### `TaskGroup` — dynamic fan-out

When the number of parallel tasks isn't known at compile time, use `withTaskGroup` to spawn tasks dynamically and collect results.

### Structured concurrency guarantees

- **Child tasks always complete before their parent scope exits** — no orphaned work.
- **Cancellation propagates**: cancelling a parent automatically cancels all children.
- Check `Task.isCancelled` at meaningful points to exit early.

```swift
func loadDashboard() async throws -> Dashboard {
    async let stats   = fetchStats()
    async let notices = fetchNotices()
    guard !Task.isCancelled else { throw CancellationError() }
    return Dashboard(stats: try await stats, notices: try await notices)
}
```

quickCheck.prompt: In structured concurrency, when do child tasks complete?
quickCheck.explanation: Structured concurrency guarantees that every child task finishes before the enclosing scope returns, preventing orphaned background work and making lifetimes predictable.

options.text: Before the parent task returns
At an indeterminate time after the parent
When the app goes to background
When the main actor is idle

questions.prompt: What does `await` actually do at runtime?
questions.explanation: `await` is a suspension point — the task pauses and the thread is released for other work. The task resumes on an appropriate executor when the result is ready.

options.text: Blocks the calling thread until the result is available
Suspends the current task and yields the thread to the scheduler
Spawns a new background thread
Converts a synchronous call to asynchronous

questions.explanation: Actors are reentrant: a suspension at `await` lets other callers execute on the actor. This means actor state can change between two awaits in the same method — guard against that.

options.text: An actor can be called from multiple actors simultaneously
While an actor is suspended at an await, another call can run on that actor
An actor retains a strong reference to itself
A method calling itself recursively inside an actor

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `Task { }` and `Task.detached { }`?
questions.explanation: `Task { }` inherits the current actor (e.g. @MainActor if called from a @MainActor context). `Task.detached` runs as a free agent — no actor inherited, useful when you explicitly don't want to capture the surrounding context.

options.text: Task.detached runs on the main thread; Task runs on a background thread
Task inherits the current actor context; Task.detached runs without any actor context
Task is structured; Task.detached is not — Task.detached's lifetime is bound to its parent
There is no functional difference

questions.prompt: What does `async let` do when you declare two bindings before awaiting them?
questions.explanation: `async let` starts both child tasks immediately in parallel. Awaiting them collects results in declaration order regardless of which finishes first.

options.text: Both tasks run in parallel — results collected in declaration order
Tasks run sequentially in declaration order
The second task doesn't start until the first is awaited
The compiler reorders them for optimal performance

questions.prompt: Why should UI updates be performed on `@MainActor`?
questions.explanation: UIKit's view hierarchy is not thread-safe — modifying views from a background thread causes undefined behavior. `@MainActor` confines code to the main thread, making safety explicit and compiler-enforced.

options.text: UIKit and SwiftUI are not thread-safe and require main-thread access
Background threads cannot access any Apple framework
@MainActor provides automatic retain counting
Only @MainActor tasks can make network calls

questions.explanation: Cancellation in Swift is cooperative — `Task.isCancelled` lets you check the flag and exit early. Tasks don't stop automatically; you must check and respond.

options.text: Immediately stops execution of the current task
true if a cancellation request has been sent to this task
Cancels all child tasks in a task group
Throws a CancellationError automatically

questions.explanation: `MainActor.run` lets non-main-actor code hop to the main actor to perform UI work in a single call, equivalent to a hopped `await` onto MainActor.

options.text: Blocks the current thread until the main actor is free
Submits a closure to run on the main actor from any context
Creates a new main-thread task
Replaces DispatchQueue.main.sync

questions.prompt: What is the problem with this code?
questions.explanation: Two concurrent tasks mutating the same variable without synchronization is a data race. Swift's strict concurrency checking would flag this; the fix is an actor or a Sendable value type.

options.text: Data race — counter is shared mutable state accessed from concurrent tasks
counter is always 2
Compile error — counter must be let
Tasks run serially so there is no race

questions.explanation: Sendable marks types safe for cross-actor or cross-task transfer. Value types are implicitly Sendable; classes must be explicitly made Sendable (usually by being immutable or internally synchronized).

options.text: A type can be sent over a network
A type is safe to pass across actor boundaries (concurrency-safe)
A type supports async/await calls
A type conforms to Codable

questions.prompt: How does Swift's structured concurrency differ from `DispatchQueue.async`?
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency ensures child tasks complete before their parent scope exits, cancellation propagates automatically, and the async/await type system enforces correct usage — things DispatchQueue cannot offer.

options.text: Structured concurrency blocks threads; DispatchQueue does not
Structured concurrency ties task lifetimes to their scope, propagates cancellation, and integrates with the type system
DispatchQueue.async supports async/await; structured concurrency does not
There is no meaningful difference
